script.opening: (Parent, with the young man) "We’re worried about Adam. His blood tests showed his liver’s not right, but he doesn’t drink much. Over the last several months his hands have started shaking, his speech is a bit slurred sometimes, and he’s become really withdrawn and moody — his college work’s fallen apart. Could it all be connected?"

facts.text: Adam (19) and his mother, Louise. Adam answers briefly and quietly; Louise does most of the talking. Louise is happy to leave the room if asked.
Bloods 3 weeks ago for tiredness: "ALT was raised — about four times normal — and they said to discuss it." No jaundice, no itching, no swollen tummy, no vomiting blood, no confusion.
Hands shaking for about 4 months — worse when writing or holding a cup; handwriting messy. Speech "a bit thick" sometimes. Drooling a little at night. Clumsier. No seizures, no headaches.

Adam: "I just feel flat." Stopped seeing friends, can’t concentrate, irritable, sleeping a lot. Failing his college course (engineering). No thoughts of self-harm if asked privately. No hallucinations.
"Honestly, barely anything." A couple of beers a month. No drugs, no steroids, no supplements. No tattoos.
Younger sister, Ellie (15), is well. An uncle (Louise’s brother) "died of liver problems in his twenties — we always thought it was drink". Parents are not related.
No regular medicines; no allergies. Healthy childhood.

Louise: worried, organised, says "People said teenage moods, but the shaking doesn’t fit." Adam: flat, slow to answer, embarrassed by the tremor. If the doctor talks to Adam directly and kindly, he engages a little more. Louise asks "Is that serious?" and Adam asks "So the mood stuff might be part of it?" and "What about college?".

ice.ideas: Louise: "Could it all be connected?" Adam: "I don’t know."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — Louise fears it is drugs or alcohol and that Adam is hiding it; she also remembers her brother’s early death. Adam fears he is "going mad" and is ashamed of failing college.
ice.expectations: "An explanation, and someone to look into it properly."

cues: "He doesn’t drink much" — the liver result is unexplained.
"People said teenage moods, but the shaking doesn’t fit" — the combination is the clue.
"My brother died of liver problems young" (if family history is asked) — a possible inherited condition.

checkpoints.text: THINKS of WILSON’S DISEASE from the COMBINATION of unexplained liver disease with neurological (tremor/dysarthria/dystonia) and/or psychiatric/behavioural features in a young person (especially under about 40, EASL–ERN 2025)
Recognises it is rare but TREATABLE and devastating if missed — not attributing the picture to alcohol, "teenage moodiness" or primary psychiatric illness alone

Knows the diagnostic clues — low serum CAERULOPLASMIN, raised urinary/hepatic copper, KAYSER-FLEISCHER rings on slit-lamp — and arranges/seeks caeruloplasmin (knowing a normal level does not exclude it) and a slit-lamp eye examination (plus LFTs with a liver aetiology screen/copper studies)
Recognises the autosomal-recessive inheritance and the need for FAMILY (sibling) SCREENING

REFERS urgently to hepatology/neurology/specialist services for confirmation and treatment (copper chelation — penicillamine/trientine — or zinc; lifelong; transplant in acute or end-stage liver failure), with same-day assessment for jaundice, confusion, drowsiness, bleeding or vomiting blood

Takes the family’s "could it all be connected?" seriously, validates their concern, and explains the plan sensitively to the young person and parent, checking Adam’s consent for his parent to be present and seeing him alone for part of the consultation
Communicates the need for specialist assessment clearly without over-alarming, and checks understanding

Safety-nets and follows up: caeruloplasmin/slit-lamp/copper studies + specialist referral, family screening, mental-health support with a self-harm risk check, liver-failure warning signs, and review — thinking of a treatable inherited cause, not dismissing it

worked.txt: "Yes — it may well all be connected, and you were right to ask. When a young person has liver problems together with a new tremor, slurred speech and changes in mood, there’s a specific condition we must consider called Wilson’s disease, where copper builds up in the body."

"It’s rare, but it’s really important because it’s treatable — and if it’s caught late it can cause lasting harm to the liver and brain. So it’s exactly the kind of thing we shouldn’t miss in someone Adam’s age."

"I’ll arrange some tests — a blood test called caeruloplasmin, repeat liver tests with a full liver screen and a liver scan, and I’d like to examine Adam in person. The specialists will do copper studies and an eye examination to look for a copper ring at the edge of the cornea, which is a classic sign. A normal caeruloplasmin wouldn’t rule it out on its own."
"I’m referring Adam to the liver and neurology specialists to confirm the diagnosis and start treatment if needed — medicines that remove or block copper, taken long-term."

"Because it runs in families, his brothers and sisters should also be checked — treating it early prevents problems. And the mood changes are part of this, not him being difficult; we’ll support that too."

"Get him seen the same day if he becomes yellow, confused or drowsy, bleeds or bruises easily, or vomits blood, and get urgent help if he has any thoughts of harming himself. Come back sooner if his mood or thinking deteriorate. I’ll get the tests and referral moving and we’ll go through the results together."

f.learning: WILSON’S DISEASE (an autosomal-recessive disorder of COPPER accumulation affecting liver and brain) should be CONSIDERED in anyone with unexplained LIVER disease — especially a YOUNG person under about 40 (EASL–ERN 2025, international) — and/or NEUROLOGICAL (tremor, dystonia, dysarthria, parkinsonism, clumsiness) and PSYCHIATRIC/behavioural (mood/personality change, cognitive decline, falling grades) features — the COMBINATION of hepatic with neuropsychiatric features being the key prompt ("could it all be connected?"). It is rare but crucially TREATABLE, and devastating (progressive liver failure, irreversible neurological/psychiatric damage, death) if missed, so it must be considered and excluded rather than attributed to alcohol, "teenage moodiness" or primary psychiatric illness alone. Diagnostic clues include a low serum CAERULOPLASMIN (a normal level does not exclude it), raised 24-hour urinary copper (and raised hepatic copper on biopsy), and KAYSER-FLEISCHER rings (copper at the corneal margin) on slit-lamp examination (especially with neurological involvement); arrange/seek caeruloplasmin and a slit-lamp eye exam alongside LFTs with a liver aetiology screen (BSG 2018) and copper studies, with genetic testing (ATP7B) supporting the diagnosis. As an autosomal-recessive condition, siblings and family should be SCREENED, since early treatment of pre-symptomatic relatives prevents disease. Refer to hepatology/neurology/specialist services for confirmation and treatment — copper chelation (penicillamine or trientine) or zinc (reduces absorption) (EASL–ERN 2025, AASLD 2022, international; BNF), with dietary copper advice only a minor supportive measure, lifelong treatment and monitoring (stopping can cause fatal liver failure), and liver transplant for acute or end-stage liver failure. Primary care’s role is to think of it, arrange initial tests, refer urgently, and arrange same-day assessment for signs of acute liver failure (jaundice, confusion, drowsiness, bleeding/bruising, vomiting blood) or haemolysis. At 19, Adam is an adult: check his consent for the parent to be present, see him alone for part of the consultation, and assess mood and self-harm risk. The skill is recognising the combined liver + neuro/psychiatric pattern in a young person, doing/arranging caeruloplasmin and a slit-lamp exam, screening family, and referring — not dismissing it.

knowledge.summary: A young man with abnormal liver tests, a new tremor, slurred speech and a change in mood and behaviour should make you think of Wilson’s disease. It is an inherited disorder of copper build-up in the liver and brain: rare, treatable, and devastating if missed. Check caeruloplasmin and liver tests, refer urgently to hepatology (and neurology) for copper studies and a slit-lamp eye examination, and plan family screening. Adam is an adult, so ask him about his parent being present, and see him alone for part of the consultation.

points.t: Unexplained liver disease together with neurological signs (tremor, dysarthria, dystonia, clumsiness, parkinsonism) or psychiatric change (mood, personality, behaviour, falling school or work performance) in a child or young adult. Consider it in anyone with unexplained liver disease, especially under about 40 [1].

Treatment stops progression and can reverse much of the damage. Untreated, it leads to cirrhosis, acute liver failure (often with haemolysis) and permanent neurological harm. Do not put the tremor down to anxiety, or the mood change to adolescence.

A low serum caeruloplasmin supports it, but a normal level does not exclude it. The specialist adds 24-hour urinary copper, a slit-lamp examination for Kayser–Fleischer rings (present in most people with neurological disease), genetic testing (ATP7B) and sometimes liver copper. Combined scoring systems such as the Leipzig score are used [1].

Repeat LFTs with a full liver aetiology screen [3]: FBC (haemolysis), clotting, albumin, U&E, hepatitis B and C serology, autoantibodies and immunoglobulins, ferritin and transferrin saturation, caeruloplasmin, and a liver ultrasound. Ask about alcohol, drugs and supplements directly with Adam.

Refer urgently to hepatology, and to neurology for the movement and speech symptoms. Arrange same-day assessment for jaundice, confusion, drowsiness, bleeding or bruising, or vomiting blood, which suggest liver failure.

Specialist-led and lifelong: chelation with penicillamine or trientine, or zinc to block absorption; chelators are preferred for significant liver disease [1, 2]. Neurological symptoms can briefly worsen when treatment starts. Stopping treatment can cause fatal liver failure, so adherence is vital. Liver transplant is used for acute liver failure or end-stage disease.

Inheritance is autosomal recessive, so brothers and sisters have a 1 in 4 chance of being affected and should be screened. Psychiatric symptoms need assessment and support in their own right, including a risk check.

Explored college, social withdrawal and mood; took a confidential alcohol, drug and supplement history alone with Adam.

Wilson’s disease versus alcohol or drug-related liver injury, viral or autoimmune hepatitis, primary psychiatric illness and other tremors.
Screened for liver failure and haemolysis; risk assessment for self-harm.
Possible Wilson’s disease, needing urgent specialist confirmation.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.

Idea: teenage moods did not fit. Concern: something serious being missed. Expectation: to know what is wrong.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Ahmed. Adam, it’s good to meet you. Are you happy for your parent to stay while we talk?
model.why: Addresses the adult patient first and checks consent

model.text: Adam: Yeah, that’s fine.
Thank you. What’s been happening?

Parent: We’re worried about Adam. His blood tests showed his liver’s not right, but he doesn’t drink much. Over the last several months his hands have started shaking, his speech is a bit slurred sometimes, and he’s become really withdrawn and moody. His college work’s fallen apart. Could it all be connected?
That’s a really good question, and I’ll come back to it. Adam, how does it seem from your side?
model.why: Brings the patient back into the conversation

model.text: Adam: I don’t know. My hands shake and it’s hard to write. I just feel flat.
When did you first notice the shaking, and is it there at rest, or when you use your hands?
Adam: A few months ago. It makes writing hard.
Any stiffness, clumsiness, trouble swallowing, or drooling?
Adam: Not really. Just the shaking and my speech sometimes.
Have you noticed yellowing of your eyes or skin, dark urine, itching, swelling of your tummy or legs, or easy bruising?
Adam: No, none of that.
Adam, I’d like to ask you a few questions on your own, which I do with all young adults. Would that be all right?
model.why: Creates space for a confidential history

model.text: Parent: Of course, I’ll wait outside.
Thanks, Adam. How much do you really drink, and do you use any drugs, supplements or anything from the gym or the internet?
model.why: Confidential alcohol, drug and supplement history

model.text: Adam: Honestly, barely anything. No drugs.
You said you feel flat. Have you had thoughts that life isn’t worth living, or of harming yourself?
Adam: No. I just can’t concentrate and I’ve stopped seeing people.
Thank you for telling me. Shall we ask your parent back in?
Adam: Yeah.
You both wondered if it’s all connected. What have you been thinking it might be?
Parent: We didn’t know. People said teenage moods, but the shaking doesn’t fit that.
What worries you most?
Parent: That something serious is being missed.
And Adam, what would you like from today?
Adam: To know what’s wrong, I suppose.
I’d like to examine you: your eyes, your tummy for the liver and spleen, your hands and the tremor, your speech, walking and coordination.
Adam: Okay.

You were right to ask whether it’s connected. When a young person has a liver problem together with a new tremor, slurred speech and a change in mood, we must think about a condition called Wilson’s disease. The body can’t get rid of copper properly, so it builds up in the liver and the brain.
model.why: Names Wilson’s disease and links the features

model.text: Parent: Is that serious?

It’s rare, and it may not be what Adam has. But it’s important to check for because it’s treatable, and treatment can stop it and often improve symptoms. If it were missed it could cause lasting damage, so I want it looked at quickly.
Adam: So the mood stuff might be part of it?
It could be. Copper can affect mood, concentration and behaviour. It isn’t you being difficult.
model.why: Validates the psychiatric symptoms as part of the illness

model.text: I’ll repeat the liver tests today with a full set of liver checks, including a blood test called caeruloplasmin, a blood count, clotting and a liver scan. I’m also referring you urgently to the liver specialists, who will do copper tests and have an eye specialist look for copper deposits at the edge of the cornea. I’ll ask neurology to see you too.
model.why: Aetiology screen, caeruloplasmin and urgent specialist referral

model.text: Parent: And if it is Wilson’s?

Treatment is with tablets that remove copper or stop it being absorbed, taken for life and supervised by the specialists. Because it runs in families, any brothers or sisters would need checking, as treating early prevents problems.
Adam: What about college?
I can write to college to explain there’s a medical problem being investigated, so they can give you some slack. And I’d like to keep an eye on your mood as we go.
model.why: Practical support and mental health follow-up

model.text: Please get seen the same day if Adam goes yellow, becomes confused or unusually drowsy, bruises or bleeds easily, vomits blood, or if his mood drops or he has any thoughts of harming himself. What will you take away from today?
Adam: Bloods and a scan, urgent liver and neurology referral, maybe an eye test. Come back quickly if I go yellow or confused, or feel worse in myself.
That’s right. I’ll call you with the blood results this week and see you again in two weeks.

social.t: Falling grades are part of the picture. A letter to college helps him get extensions and support while he is investigated.
Parents often feel guilt about missing signs, or about passing on a gene. Acknowledge this if the diagnosis is confirmed.

legal.t: At 19, Adam is an adult. He decides who is present and what is shared. Seeing him alone for part of the consultation respects his confidentiality (GMC Confidentiality, 2017).
If cognitive or psychiatric change became severe, assess capacity for specific decisions under the Mental Capacity Act 2005.

professional.t: Labelling neuropsychiatric change as adolescence or mental illness can delay the diagnosis. Consider physical causes when features do not fit.
Screening relatives needs Adam’s consent to share his diagnosis. Discuss this with him and the specialist team.

community.t: Patient support organisations for Wilson’s disease and for liver conditions, such as the British Liver Trust, offer information for families.

redFlags: Jaundice, confusion, drowsiness, bleeding or bruising: possible acute liver failure
Rapidly worsening speech, swallowing or walking
Self-harm thoughts or severe mood change
psychosocial: Social withdrawal and falling college work
ice: Expectation: to know what is wrong

playbook.diagnosis: Possible Wilson’s disease: abnormal liver tests with an action tremor, dysarthria and neuropsychiatric change in a 19-year-old. Other liver causes and a primary psychiatric illness to be considered.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “There’s a rare condition called Wilson’s disease, where copper builds up in the liver and brain. It could explain the liver tests, the shaking, the speech and the mood. It’s treatable, so we need to check for it quickly.”

management.reflectIce: “You asked whether it’s all connected. It may well be, and that’s exactly why we’re checking for Wilson’s disease.”
management.psychosocial: Adam’s consent and confidential time; college letter; mood follow-up.
sharedPlan: Repeat LFTs with liver aetiology screen, caeruloplasmin, FBC, clotting, liver ultrasound
Urgent hepatology referral for copper studies, slit-lamp examination and genetics
Neurology referral for tremor and dysarthria
Family screening if confirmed; lifelong specialist treatment
safetyNet: Same-day assessment for jaundice, confusion, drowsiness, bleeding or vomiting blood
Results this week; review in two weeks

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by solving three small problems instead of one big one. The marks are for joining the dots and getting the right specialist quickly.

items.fail: Treating the liver, tremor and mood as separate problems.
items.why: The combination in a young person is the prompt for Wilson’s disease.
items.fix: Ask yourself what single diagnosis links them.

items.fail: Blaming alcohol without a confidential history.
items.why: He may not speak freely in front of a parent, and it may not be alcohol.
items.fix: See him alone and take a full alcohol, drug and supplement history.

items.why: Delay risks liver failure and permanent neurological damage.
items.fix: Caeruloplasmin with a liver screen, then urgent hepatology referral.

items.why: Siblings have a 1 in 4 risk and benefit from early treatment.
items.fix: Mention screening of brothers and sisters.

items.why: Adam is an adult and the patient.
items.fix: Check his consent and address him directly.

items.fail: No liver-failure or mood safety net.
items.why: Acute liver failure and self-harm are the dangerous outcomes.
items.fix: Give specific red flags and a review date.

Adam is an adult, so ask him about his parent being present, and see him alone for part of the consultation.

points.t: Unexplained liver disease together with neurological signs (tremor, dysarthria, dystonia, clumsiness, parkinsonism) or psychiatric change (mood, personality, behaviour, falling school or work performance) in a child or young adult. Consider it in anyone with unexplained liver disease, especially under about 40 [1].

Treatment stops progression and can reverse much of the damage. Untreated, it leads to cirrhosis, acute liver failure (often with haemolysis) and permanent neurological harm. Do not put the tremor down to anxiety, or the mood change to adolescence.

A low serum caeruloplasmin supports it, but a normal level does not exclude it. The specialist adds 24-hour urinary copper, a slit-lamp examination for Kayser–Fleischer rings (present in most people with neurological disease), genetic testing (ATP7B) and sometimes liver copper. Combined scoring systems such as the Leipzig score are used [1].

Repeat LFTs with a full liver aetiology screen [3]: FBC (haemolysis), clotting, albumin, U&E, hepatitis B and C serology, autoantibodies and immunoglobulins, ferritin and transferrin saturation, caeruloplasmin, and a liver ultrasound. Ask about alcohol, drugs and supplements directly with Adam.

Refer urgently to hepatology, and to neurology for the movement and speech symptoms. Arrange same-day assessment for jaundice, confusion, drowsiness, bleeding or bruising, or vomiting blood, which suggest liver failure.

Specialist-led and lifelong: chelation with penicillamine or trientine, or zinc to block absorption; chelators are preferred for significant liver disease [1, 2]. Neurological symptoms can briefly worsen when treatment starts. Stopping treatment can cause fatal liver failure, so adherence is vital. Liver transplant is used for acute liver failure or end-stage disease.

Inheritance is autosomal recessive, so brothers and sisters have a 1 in 4 chance of being affected and should be screened. Psychiatric symptoms need assessment and support in their own right, including a risk check.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Checked Adam’s consent for his parent to stay; open question; heard both the parent’s concern and Adam’s own account.
Explored college, social withdrawal and mood; took a confidential alcohol, drug and supplement history alone with Adam.
Picked up ‘could it all be connected?’ as the key cue linking the liver, tremor, speech and mood.
Idea: teenage moods did not fit. Concern: something serious being missed. Expectation: to know what is wrong.
Examined for jaundice, liver and spleen, tremor, speech, gait and coordination; LFTs, liver aetiology screen with caeruloplasmin, FBC, clotting, liver ultrasound.
Wilson’s disease versus alcohol or drug-related liver injury, viral or autoimmune hepatitis, primary psychiatric illness and other tremors.
Screened for liver failure and haemolysis; risk assessment for self-harm.
Possible Wilson’s disease, needing urgent specialist confirmation.
Urgent hepatology referral for copper studies and slit-lamp examination; neurology referral; lifelong treatment outlined.
Family screening explained; mood support; college letter.
Same-day help for jaundice, confusion, drowsiness, bleeding or self-harm thoughts; results this week; review in two weeks.

social.t: Falling grades are part of the picture. A letter to college helps him get extensions and support while he is investigated.
Parents often feel guilt about missing signs, or about passing on a gene. Acknowledge this if the diagnosis is confirmed.

legal.t: At 19, Adam is an adult. He decides who is present and what is shared. Seeing him alone for part of the consultation respects his confidentiality (GMC Confidentiality, 2017).
If cognitive or psychiatric change became severe, assess capacity for specific decisions under the Mental Capacity Act 2005.

professional.t: Labelling neuropsychiatric change as adolescence or mental illness can delay the diagnosis. Consider physical causes when features do not fit.
Screening relatives needs Adam’s consent to share his diagnosis. Discuss this with him and the specialist team.

community.t: Patient support organisations for Wilson’s disease and for liver conditions, such as the British Liver Trust, offer information for families.

redFlags: Jaundice, confusion, drowsiness, bleeding or bruising: possible acute liver failure
Rapidly worsening speech, swallowing or walking
Self-harm thoughts or severe mood change

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by solving three small problems instead of one big one. The marks are for joining the dots and getting the right specialist quickly.

items.fail: Treating the liver, tremor and mood as separate problems.
items.why: The combination in a young person is the prompt for Wilson’s disease.
items.fix: Ask yourself what single diagnosis links them.

items.fail: Blaming alcohol without a confidential history.
items.why: He may not speak freely in front of a parent, and it may not be alcohol.
items.fix: See him alone and take a full alcohol, drug and supplement history.

items.why: Delay risks liver failure and permanent neurological damage.
items.fix: Caeruloplasmin with a liver screen, then urgent hepatology referral.

items.why: Siblings have a 1 in 4 risk and benefit from early treatment.
items.fix: Mention screening of brothers and sisters.

items.why: Adam is an adult and the patient.
items.fix: Check his consent and address him directly.

items.fail: No liver-failure or mood safety net.
items.why: Acute liver failure and self-harm are the dangerous outcomes.
items.fix: Give specific red flags and a review date.
